opus-5.5.text:
I think a lot of what we actually care about, like real scientific discovery, building complex systems, or understanding something new about the world, isn't done in one shot. When you look at how a researcher makes progress, it's rarely a single flash of insight. It's days, weeks, sometimes years of sustained effort: trying an approach, seeing it fail, figuring out why, keeping track of what you've learned, and slowly building toward something. So if we want models that can meaningfully contribute to that kind of work, they need to be able to stay on a problem coherently for a long time.

What's been exciting is that the time horizon over which models can work productively has been growing quite steadily. Not long ago these systems were good at answering a question in a few seconds. Now, with reasoning models, we see them think for minutes or hours, explore different paths, notice their own mistakes, and come back. That's a qualitatively different capability, and it seems to keep scaling as we put more compute into it.

There's also a practical reason. Many of the hardest problems don't need a broad, shallow assistant. They need depth: a lot of focused thinking on one specific question. If you can give a model a well-defined, hard problem and let it work for a long time, you can start getting results that would take a human expert a very long time, or that we might not get at all. I think that's where we'll first see AI making truly novel contributions, in areas like math, science, and AI research itself.

And of course, it raises important questions. When a model works autonomously for a long stretch, you need to understand what it's doing and make sure it's pursuing the goal you intended. So alongside capability, we spend a lot of thought on how to keep that process understandable and aligned. But as a direction, I think sustained, focused work is one of the clearest paths to AI that genuinely expands what we know.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the simplest way to put it is that the hardest and most valuable problems humans work on are not things you solve in a few seconds. A mathematician might spend months or years on a single conjecture. A research team might spend a decade on a scientific question. And when we look at what models have been able to do historically, they were really good at tasks that take a human a few seconds or a few minutes—answer a question, write a function, summarize a document. The gap between that and what we actually care about, which is genuinely new science, new engineering, is mostly a gap in how long a model can stay productively engaged with one problem.

So when we track the time horizon of tasks models can complete, it's been extending quite steadily. A couple of years ago it was minutes, then hours, and now we're seeing models carry a line of reasoning across something that would take a person days. What's interesting is that it's not just doing more steps. Working for a long time requires a set of capabilities that you don't need for short tasks: you have to keep track of what you've tried, notice when an approach is failing, back out and try something different, verify your own intermediate results, and sometimes revise your understanding of the problem itself. Those are the skills that distinguish research from answering questions.

The reason I find it so promising is that it's a very clean axis to measure and to improve. If a model can reliably make progress on a problem for a week, then the question of what it can discover becomes mostly a question of compute and of how many of these you run. And I think that's where we start seeing AI not just assisting with research but actually doing some of it—producing results that a person would be proud of having found. That's the thing I care most about, and the ability to stay focused for a long time is, I think, the main bottleneck between here and there.

astra-6.text:
I think it opens up a different dimension of what these systems can do. A lot of our interaction with models today is asking a question and getting an answer within seconds. But many of the problems we care about don’t have answers that you can produce in seconds, even if you’re very capable. You need to explore different approaches, test your assumptions, find mistakes, and revise your thinking.

If a model can stay focused on a problem for hours or days and make useful progress throughout that time, then we can start giving it much more substantial tasks. Scientific research is a natural example, but so is building a complicated piece of software.

The important part is that working longer actually leads to better results. Simply producing more text isn’t enough. The model needs to recognize when an approach isn’t working, check its work, and try something else. If we can get that right, I think it could substantially expand the range of problems AI can help us solve.

sol-6.1.text:
One reason is that many of the problems we care about are hard even if you have a lot of knowledge. You have to try an approach, see where it fails, revise it, and keep going. That’s true of writing software, doing research, or working through a difficult mathematical problem.

So I think there’s a very interesting direction where progress comes from models being able to sustain that process. Can a model make useful progress for an hour, or a day, while keeping track of the goal, checking its work, and recovering from mistakes?

What makes this promising is that additional computation can then translate into better answers. You don’t have to solve everything in one immediate response. But simply running longer isn’t enough—you need the model to use that time productively. If we can make that reliable, it could expand the range of problems these systems can help us solve.
